items.prompt: Which ring means the team has real production experience and stands behind the technology?
choices: Adopt
Trial
Assess
items.explanation: Adopt is the default choice backed by real production experience.

items.prompt: Which ring is meant for a spike kept away from anything critical?
choices: Adopt, the default ring
Assess
Hold, for old tools
items.explanation: Assess builds understanding without committing the team.

items.prompt: What does a Hold entry tell a newcomer about new work?
choices: Use it as the default
Run it on a bounded project
Start nothing new with it
items.explanation: Hold means known problems or a deliberate step back; existing use is tolerated, not encouraged.

items.prompt: What does Trial mean?
choices: A real project uses it, with limits
It is the default for all new work
It was only read about in a blog post
items.explanation: Trial is real use with limits, and it is not yet proven.

items.prompt: Must every technology climb Assess, then Trial, then Adopt?
choices: No, entries may stop early
Yes, the order is fixed
Yes, but only in small teams
items.explanation: The rings are not a ladder. Entries can stop at any ring.

items.prompt: A newcomer wants the safe default for a new service. Which ring do they look in?
choices: Assess
Hold
Adopt
items.explanation: Adopt is the default for new work in its category.

items.prompt: Can an Adopt entry later move to Hold?
choices: No, Adopt entries are permanent
Yes, if circumstances change
Only after a full year of use
items.explanation: Any ring can fall back to Hold when the situation changes.

items.prompt: A technology was only seen at a conference talk. Which ring fits best?
choices: Adopt, as the default choice
Assess
Trial, on a bounded project
items.explanation: Nothing has been tried on a real project, so at most it is worth assessing.

items.prompt: A tool has run one small production project for two months with no incidents. Which ring describes it best?
choices: Trial: it has real use, but in a bounded project
Adopt: two quiet months prove it is the default
Assess: production use is still only a spike
Hold: no incident yet means no evidence either way
items.explanation: Trial fits real, bounded use. One quiet project has not shown how the tool fails, so it is not yet the default.
items.reference:
Four rings, four promises
Adopt: production experience, default choice
Trial: real but bounded project
Assess: spike, nothing critical
Hold: no new work, existing use tolerated
Why: a ring tells a reader how committed the team is, and so what they may do with the technology.
items.learnMore:
The four rings

Each ring is a promise about commitment. Entries are not required to climb: most stop at Assess or Trial, and any entry can fall back to Hold.

Common mistake

Treating the rings as a ladder everything must climb, so an entry stuck in Trial looks like a failure instead of an honest answer.
items.reflection: Think of the tools or habits in your own household or hobby. Which would you put in each of the four rings, and which are you only assessing?

items.prompt: Four services use a library whose maintainers have stopped releasing fixes. What should its ring say?
choices: Assess: the team should spike it again
Adopt: four services already depend on it
Trial: the team should now bound its use
Hold: existing use stays, nothing new
items.explanation: Hold tolerates existing use while telling everyone not to extend it.

items.reference:
Ring and quadrant answer different questions
Ring: how sure are we?
Quadrant: what kind of thing is it?
Techniques, Tools, Platforms, Languages & Frameworks
No shared map: sprawl
Why: two coordinates per entry stop unlike things being compared and make quiet adoption visible.
items.learnMore:
Quadrants and sprawl

The quadrant groups entries by kind, so a practice is not compared with a platform. The ring then says how committed the team is within that kind. Together they make quiet, local adoption visible.

Common mistake

Treating the radar as an approval committee. It is a shared, living record, and it never blocks anyone from trying something.
items.reflection: Where in your own work or life do choices pile up quietly without anyone deciding? What would a one-page shared map of them look like?

items.prompt: What should move an entry forward a ring?
choices: Evidence from using it
A convincing pitch
A popular conference talk
items.explanation: Rings move on use, not on persuasion.

items.prompt: What does the Assess to Trial move ask?
choices: Did the spike show any dealbreaker?
Did everyone vote for it this week?
Is it the newest option?
items.explanation: A spike either surfaces a dealbreaker or it does not.

items.prompt: What does Trial to Adopt need?
choices: A project that survived a failure
A second demo to the team
A written wish from one engineer or lead
items.explanation: Adopt needs operating experience including a failure.

items.prompt: Which of these can justify Adopt to Hold?
choices: Upstream is no longer maintained
The logo was redesigned last year
A new engineer dislikes it
items.explanation: Responsibility to recommend it has gone.

items.prompt: What should Hold to Assess require?
choices: Someone hoping it is fixed
The cause really changed
A year passing
items.explanation: Hope is not evidence that conditions changed.

items.prompt: A 2-day spike went well. What is the sensible next ring?
choices: Adopt for all new work now
Trial on a small project
Hold until next year
items.explanation: A spike supports a Trial, not the default.

items.prompt: A spike shows a licensing dealbreaker. What happens to the entry?
choices: It moves to Adopt anyway
It moves to Trial instead
It is dropped
items.explanation: A dealbreaker ends the Assess stage.

items.prompt: Without a question per move, who tends to win?
choices: The loudest advocate
The oldest technology
The cheapest option
items.explanation: Without evidence rules, ring changes follow persuasion.

items.prompt: A six-week Trial ran smoothly, but nothing ever went wrong. Should it move to Adopt?
choices: Not yet: no failure has been survived
Yes: six smooth weeks are strong evidence
Yes: Trial always ends in Adopt after a month
No: Trial entries can never be adopted
items.explanation: Adopt needs the team to have survived an actual failure mode, which smooth weeks cannot show.
items.reference:
One question per ring move
Assess → Trial: any dealbreaker?
Trial → Adopt: survived a real failure?
Adopt → Hold: still responsible to recommend?
Hold → Assess: did conditions actually change?
Why: an explicit question per move stops the loudest advocate winning by default.
items.learnMore:
Evidence per transition

Each ring exists to answer a question. The move happens when that question has a concrete answer from using the technology, not from a good pitch.

Common mistake

Counting enthusiasm, votes or a good demo as evidence. Only what happened when the technology was used counts.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you made on enthusiasm. What single question would you have asked first, and what would have counted as an answer?

Keep it on Hold and never look at it again
Ask what changed, and check the new terms yourself
items.explanation: Hold to Assess needs the condition to have really changed, which is a checkable fact.

items.prompt: What happens to staleness as the gap between reviews grows?

items.prompt: A radar was last reviewed two years ago. What is the problem?
choices: It has too few quadrants

Its entries have gone stale
items.explanation: Value decays like any cached decision.

items.prompt: Why not review the radar every day?

It becomes background noise
Quadrants would all be lost
items.explanation: A review should be a real, scheduled conversation.

items.prompt: Using the unit's model (months × change rate × 2.2, capped at 100), what staleness does a 6-month gap give at change rate 4?
items.explanation: 6 × 4 × 2.2 = 52.8, below the cap.
items.reference:
A radar decays like a cached decision
Modelled staleness = months × change rate (of 10) × 2.2, capped at 100
6 months at rate 4: 52.8%
Quarterly is a practical middle
Security issues need an out-of-band trigger
Why: every entry is a snapshot, so the longer the gap, the more of the radar is wrong.
items.learnMore:
Review cadence

A radar is only as fresh as its last review. Teams use a routine cadence, often quarterly, for ordinary drift, plus an immediate trigger for security disclosures and abandoned upstreams. The staleness figures here come from the unit's illustrative model, not measurements.

Common mistake

Treating the schedule as enough. A vulnerability found the week after a review would otherwise mislead readers for months.
items.reflection: What in your own life is a snapshot that quietly goes out of date, such as a budget or a contact list? What routine and what trigger would keep it honest?

choices: How much each criterion matters
How many engineers voted on it
How old each candidate is
items.explanation: Weights are the team's priorities made explicit.

items.prompt: Which candidate won the worked example?
choices: Kafka, the most mature
Hosted SQS
NATS, the simplest
items.explanation: Hosted SQS scored 7.6 against 5.9 and 4.3.

items.prompt: In this unit, what does a migration cost score of 10 mean?
choices: Cheap to adopt
Very expensive to adopt
Already adopted
items.explanation: The criterion is scored so higher is better.

items.prompt: Two engineers use identical sub-scores but pick different winners. What differs?
choices: Their sub-scores
Their weights
Their candidates
items.explanation: With the same sub-scores only the weights can differ.

items.prompt: When should the sub-scores be set?
choices: Before anyone has tried it
After the decision is made
After a real spike
items.explanation: Scores need evidence from the Assess stage.

items.prompt: Is 5.6 against 5.9 a decisive gap?
choices: No, too close to settle alone
Yes, the higher number always wins
Yes, but only for Kafka
items.explanation: A close score leaves room for qualitative factors.

items.prompt: Kafka has the highest maturity score. Why does it still score lowest?
choices: Its familiarity and cost scores are low
Maturity is not counted in the score
Its strategic fit score is exactly zero
items.explanation: Weighted low scores on two criteria outweigh its maturity.

items.prompt: What is Hosted SQS's weighted score in the worked example?
A team scores three tools from blog posts before trying any of them. What is the main weakness?
choices: The sub-scores are unevidenced guesses
The weights should have been equal for all tools
The score cannot be used with three candidates
Blog posts always favour the oldest tool
items.explanation: Garbage in, garbage out: the score is only as good as the evidence behind the sub-scores.
items.reference:
Score = sum of weight × sub-score
Weights: 0.3 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.2
Kafka 4.3, NATS 5.9, Hosted SQS 7.6
Same sub-scores, different winner: weights differ
Close score: judgment decides
Why: the table exposes disagreement about weights, but its numbers are only as good as the evidence behind the sub-scores.
items.learnMore:
Scoring candidates

A weighted score forces the team to agree on weights out loud and to score each candidate after a real spike. It structures judgment and does not replace it, and a close score should be settled by the factors the table cannot see.

Common mistake

Treating a precise-looking number as objective. Guessed sub-scores multiplied by agreed weights are still guesses.
items.reflection: Think of a choice you made between options, such as a place to live or a course. Which criterion carried the most weight for you, and would a friend have weighted it differently?

items.prompt: Two candidates score 5.8 and 5.9. How should the team proceed?
choices: Pick 5.9, because the table has spoken
Re-run it with weights until one wins by 2
Call it a tie and use what the table misses
Pick the candidate with the highest maturity
items.explanation: A near tie is within the noise of subjective sub-scores.

Why: the table exposes disagreement about weights, but its numbers are only as good as the evidence behind the sub-scores.
items.learnMore:
Scoring candidates

A weighted score forces the team to agree on weights out loud and to score each candidate after a real spike. It structures judgment and does not replace it, and a close score should be settled by the factors the table cannot see.

Common mistake

Treating a precise-looking number as objective. Guessed sub-scores multiplied by agreed weights are still guesses.
items.reflection: Think of a choice you made between options, such as a place to live or a course. Which criterion carried the most weight for you, and would a friend have weighted it differently?
